# Ballistics and scientific gunnery (`ballistics_gunnery`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs cannon_artillery; helped by falling_bodies, trigonometry, laws_of_motion, calculus
- Core idea: A shot follows a curve set by its muzzle speed, the elevation of the barrel, gravity and air resistance. In a vacuum the path is a parabola with greatest range at 45 degrees, but at gun speeds air resistance is many times the weight of the ball, so real ranges are far shorter and the best elevation is lower. Robins measured muzzle speed by firing into a heavy pendulum and reading its swing, and showed that a spinning ball curves sideways. Practical gunnery needs a quadrant to set elevation, range tables made by trial for each gun and charge, and balls and charges of constant weight.
- Pitfalls:
  - Teaching the vacuum parabola as if it were true for guns; it overestimates range several times over
  - Tartaglia's and Aristotle's picture of a straight flight followed by a sudden drop is wrong
  - Range tables are useless if powder strength and ball size vary from shot to shot
  - A smoothbore ball leaves the muzzle with random spin, so no theory makes it accurate at long range
- History: europe: 1537 – Tartaglia, Nova scientia, gunner's quadrant and the 45 degree rule; 1638 – Galileo's parabola; 1742 – Benjamin Robins, ballistic pendulum; 1745 – Euler's German edition with mathematical commentary; 1753 – Euler's equations for flight with air resistance; china: 1044 – Wujing Zongyao gives empirical ranges for trebuchets and crossbows; 17th c. – Jesuit-taught gunnery at the Ming and Qing courts; islamic: 16th c. – Ottoman gunners use quadrant and sight empirically
- Read:
  - Benjamin Robins, New Principles of Gunnery (1742)
  - A. R. Hall, Ballistics in the Seventeenth Century (1952)
  - Brett D. Steele, Muskets and Pendulums: Benjamin Robins, Leonhard Euler, and the Ballistics Revolution, Technology and Culture 35 (1994)
